title: Areas of Confusion in Cognitive Science, Part 1
author: Firth, Jonathan
source: Jonathan Firth's Memory and Metacognition Updates
summary: Jonathan Firth catalogues common misconceptions within cognitive science itself -- not just the well-known neuromyths of popular culture but distortions of genuinely valid ideas from within the research tradition. He invokes Haertel's concept of 'lethal mutations': modifications of a research-based idea that change it enough to harm efficacy or produce harm. Firth focuses first on retrieval practice, arguing that the idea has been so thoroughly assimilated into teacher practice that its original research basis is now misunderstood: teachers may be doing procedures labeled 'retrieval practice' that miss the essential cognitive conditions. The article also notes the left-brain/right-brain myth as a case of how real hemispheric research becomes a misleading personality categorization. This is framed as part 1 of a multi-part series, setting up more areas of confusion to follow. Firth's central concern is that the success of cognitive science in education creates its own epistemic risk: widespread adoption of labels without the understanding needed to implement the underlying principles correctly.
points: Cognitive science is not immune to its own myths: valuable research ideas can be distorted and misunderstood within the teaching profession in ways that harm their efficacy -- what Haertel calls 'lethal mutations.'

Retrieval practice has become so embedded in teacher practice that the label is now applied to activities that miss the essential cognitive conditions -- the difficulty-driven memory-strengthening mechanism -- making it the most practically urgent area of confusion.

The left-brain/right-brain categorization illustrates how real neuroscience (genuine hemispheric differences in function) becomes an oversimplified and unhelpful personality typology that distorts the underlying science.

The pattern across cases is that a kernel of real research -- retrieval advantage, hemispheric specialization -- gets simplified and reified until it becomes a category error that practitioners rely on without questioning.

Firth's project is to map these areas of confusion not to dismiss cognitive science in education but to protect its integrity -- ensuring that wide adoption doesn't hollow out the core of what makes the research useful.
quotes: For example, the idea that some people are 'right brained' draws on some real differences between the left and right sides of the human brain, but extend this into an oversimplified and unhelpful way of categorising people, distorting the basic science (Hines, 1987 [ ]). Cognitive science myths Unfortunately, cognitive science is not immune to myths of its own.

I thought I'd contribute to this discussion with my own take on misconceptions about cognitive science that I've noticed. Some of these might not be true lethal mutations (you can be the judge), but they strike me as significant oversimplifications of cognition research.

I perceive a popular misconception, however, in conflating retrieval practice with tests. It seems that many people forget that that things like classroom questioning and discussions lead to retrieval (if structured properly).

Perhaps the term is the problem - the term 'compare and contrast effect' has been used in some research papers, and might be a better name for it. The key idea is that interleaving needs to contrast relevant examples so that students see the difference between them.

The key idea which makes sense, and which most people get, is that working memory is limited and can be overloaded, and it makes sense to manage how much we ask learners to think about at a given time. The problem lies when simplification and reduction of content is seen as always desirable.
These should not be cut out, and we shouldn't be aiming for learning to feel easy. I've also observed a lot of educators misunderstand the timescale of cognitive load.

Perhaps you can suggest some more - if so, I'll endeavour to cover those, too! Hope you have a great week, Jonathan As a bit of further reading, here is a post I wrote a while ago about the left brain vs. right brain myth, mentioned above: Firth, J. (2021).
